theory.text: So far we've talked about the four ingredients separately. Here we see them at work together — or missing together. The difference between a prompt that works and one that wastes half an hour is never a single element: it's the combination of imprecisions that add up until the result is unusable.

bad.label: 🚧 Bad prompt
bad.content:
"Build an authentication system"
No context about the project
Stack not specified
No constraint on what not to touch
No indication of output format

good.label: 🏛️ Good prompt
good.content:
"Implement magic link authentication"
"Stack: Next.js 15 + Supabase Auth"
"Redirect to /dashboard after login"
"DO NOT touch layout in /app/layout.tsx"
"Code only, one comment per function"

theory.text: The bad prompt isn't wrong — it's incomplete. The AI will produce something, probably with JWT written from scratch, an invented database schema, and a redirect flow that has nothing to do with your project. Not because it failed: it filled every gap you left open. The good prompt leaves no gaps on any of the dimensions that matter.

theory.prompt: Implement magic link authentication. Stack: Next.js 15 + Supabase Auth. Redirect to /dashboard after login. DO NOT touch the existing layout in /app/layout.tsx. Code only, one comment per function.
theory.output:
I've created three files:
- /app/login/page.tsx — form with email field and submit button
- /app/auth/callback/route.ts — route handler for the post-login redirect
- /lib/supabase/client.ts — pre-configured Supabase client

I did not modify /app/layout.tsx. The entire flow uses native Supabase Auth — no additional libraries.

theory.text: ⚠️ A bad prompt doesn't produce an error — it produces something plausible but wrong. That's the most dangerous kind of output: it looks like it works, then you discover it doesn't integrate with anything you already have.

There's an even more powerful version of this approach: instead of writing a single good prompt, you build a chain of good prompts in sequence, where the output of each becomes the context for the next. It's the technique that unlocks truly complex tasks — and we'll see it in the next lesson.
🔑 A good prompt has context, precise task, constraints and format. Missing one is tolerable. Missing three means starting over.

exercise.prompt_template: A [BLANK] prompt doesn't produce an error — it produces something plausible but [BLANK]. It's the hardest kind of output to catch.

blanks.hint_1: What do you call a prompt that's missing context, constraints and format?
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'vague' (or 'incomplete'). A vague prompt doesn't fail obviously — it generates output that looks correct but doesn't fit the real project.

blanks.hint_1: What do you call output that looks like it works but doesn't integrate with anything?
blanks.hint_2: Not broken — just not what you needed.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'wrong' (or 'unusable'). The AI did its job — but without the right information, it worked toward a different goal than yours.

outro.recap: The difference between a bad and a good prompt isn't a single ingredient: it's the sum of imprecisions that make the output plausible but unusable.
outro.next_prompt: Next lesson: prompt chaining — how to link prompts in sequence to build complex features step by step.
